item.title: Native Rectangular Linear Assignment with Implicit Rejection: A Jonker-Volgenant Solver without Square Expansion
item.description: arXiv:2610.35948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tracking and matching applications often solve rectangular assignment with a uniform penalty for leaving elements unmatched. Widely used tracking interfaces embed the $N \times M$ costs in an (N+M)-square matrix: for 256 rows and 4096 columns, 144.5 MiB of costs for an 8 MiB problem. We describe a Jonker-Volgenant implementation that keeps the real matrix and represents rejection inside its shortest-path search by one terminal distance and one predecessor row. Building on established rectangular and optional-assignment formulations, we derive the one-sided objective and its primal-dual certificate. Rust (JVRUST), hybrid Rust/C++ (JVHYBRID), and C++ (JVCPP) implementations with native batching agree with exhaustive enumeration and are compared with expanded solvers and an exact capped-cost SciPy formulation. Two environments, Python 3.14.9 and 3.11.17 on one Intel/Windows host, each provide 8,946 timing samples across 204 cases, including 5000-square matrices, extreme aspect ratios, structured costs, and rejection sweeps. JVRUST beats capped SciPy in the same nine of ten formulation cases; JVRUST and JVCPP each preserve their ordering against the relevant SciPy baseline in all 201 non-batch cases. Congestion remains a counterexample: capped SciPy is about 9.4 and 9.1 times faster at $1024 \times 1280$. For small problems, JVRUST's four-worker batching improves on its sequential Python loop by 5.1 and 4.7 times. Repeated memory measurements confirm the cost of square expansion and an orientation-dependent native footprint. These results characterize particular implementations and software environments; they do not isolate a Python-version or programming-language effect.
item.dc:creator: Ratha Siv

item.title: diff-soup: GPU-native Differentiable Simulation and Inference for Large-scale Stiff Dynamical Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.37333v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning physical models from spatiotemporal data requires simulating systems of partial differential equations (PDEs) and differentiating through their solution. Upon spatial discretization, these models give rise to stiff dynamical systems that require repeatedly solving large, sparse linear systems. Traditional scientific computing frameworks are largely CPU-based and require problem-specific tuning to accelerate, scale, and differentiate. In this work, we introduce diff-soup, a differentiable, sparse-oriented, unified PDE suite for GPU-native simulation and inference of large, stiff dynamical systems. Built in JAX, diff-soup provides 1) a fully differentiable design for problems with sparse structure, 2) scaling to large problems through the NVIDIA cuDSS sparse direct solver with model and data multi-GPU parallelism, and 3) end-to-end PDE-constrained optimization, from classical statistical inference to embedded deep learning. On stiff PDE benchmarks, diff-soup outperforms established CPU- and GPU-based frameworks by one to two orders of magnitude in both forward solves and gradients. We demonstrate both a classical Bayesian inference workflow, identifying constitutive relationships, and a modern deep learning workflow, training a neural field for the catalyst activity of a three-dimensional packed bed reactor. We provide diff-soup as an open-source repository to facilitate research in computational science and engineering.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Degnan-Morgenstern, Martin Z. Bazant

item.title: Building Mathematical Software -- Lessons from the Development of GAP
item.description: arXiv:2610.36300v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mathematical software has particular needs that are not all covered by the existing literature on software engineering or algorithm design. This paper looks at some of these aspects, in the concrete context of the computer algebra system GAP. It also studies the potential impact AI systems could have on the development process for mathematical software.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Hulpke

item.title: Automatic Certified Differentiation in Lean
item.description: arXiv:2610.36396v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automatic differentiation (the automatic computation of numerical function derivatives) has many applications, especially in scientific computing and machine learning. Several approaches to automate the calculation of derivatives have been presented. Common challenges facing those approaches include (1) having to define derivative rules for different classes of functions, (2) having to manipulate program symbols to understand the semantics of the function being differentiated, and construct the derivative function, and (3), more importantly, ensuring that the calculated derivative is correct. In this paper, we present an approach for automatic \emph{certified} differentiation using the Lean proof assistant. By certified, we mean a correctness certificate is computed together with the derivative function and a domain on which the derivative is guaranteed to be valid. Our approach leverages existing derivative theorems included in the Mathlib Lean library instead of having to define our own rules. We also utilize Lean metaprogramming to manipulate the symbolic structure of the input function, and to construct the derivative function. The correctness certificate is computed step-wise as we apply Mathlib theorems. To make the search efficient, we index the derivative theorems by the function they differentiate. We evaluate our approach on 500 randomly generated functions: with the index, all of them are differentiated, with a median time of 0.18\,s per function, 8.6 times faster than without the index.
item.dc:creator: Ramy Shahin

item.title: A derivative-free trust-region approach for Low Order-Value Optimization problems
item.description: arXiv:2511.20783v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Low Order-Value Optimization (LOVO) problem involves minimizing the minimum among a finite number of function values within a feasible set. LOVO has several practical applications such as robust parameter estimation, protein alignment, portfolio optimization, among others. In this work, we are interested in the constrained nonlinear optimization LOVO problem of minimizing the minimum between a finite number of function values subject to a nonempty closed convex set where each function is a black-box and continuously differentiable, but the derivatives are not available. We develop the first derivative-free trust-region algorithm for constrained LOVO problems with convergence to weakly critical points. Under suitable conditions, we establish the global convergence of the algorithm and also its worst-case iteration complexity analysis. An initial open-source implementation using only linear interpolation models is developed. Extensive numerical experiments and comparison with existing alternatives show the properties and the efficiency of the proposed approach when solving LOVO problems.
item.dc:creator: Anderson E. Schwertner, Francisco N. C. Sobral
